verdicts.trueWording: Tactically speaking, I'd say go ahead and crowd in the first draft -- put everything in. Then in revising decide what counts and what tells; then cut and recombine until what's left is what counts. Leap boldly.
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (HTTP 200, browser UA). Block quote from Steering the Craft ch.10 in a Daily Kos diary by 'not a lamb'; the quoted fragment is verbatim (page uses a typographic apostrophe in "what's"; words identical). Both limbs -- crowd in the first draft, then cut and recombine -- are on the page in that order.

verdicts.trueWording: and then cut the word count by half, while "keeping the narrative clear and the sensory impact vivid."
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched. The blogger reports the ch.10 exercise: choose a past passage (~400 words) and cut the word count by half. 'Halves the word count' and the quoted proviso are both explicit and verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: Le Guin covers many of the expected topics - how to adjust sound and syntax, how to marshal adjectives and adverbs, how to control verb tense and point of view
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched. Review by Kristen Tate on thebluegarret.com (Jun 23, 2019). Quote verbatim; the full topic list in the claim (sound/syntax, adjectives/adverbs, verb tense, point of view) matches the sentence exactly.

verdicts.trueWording: hear the parallel construction of the two rhyming sets of steel and wheel and of tractor and reactor
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched. Bylined 'By Matt Bell', Reactor (formerly Tor.com), Aug 24 2021. The sentence analysed is explicitly from 'her 1966 debut Rocannon's World'. Quote verbatim; 'two rhyming word-sets' = 'the two rhyming sets'.

verdicts.trueWording: What an exquisitely well-built sentence! See the two progressions expanding its scale as it goes, its scope expanding from hundred to thousands of worlds
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched. Same Rocannon's World sentence as index 213 (adjacent clauses of one sentence). Quote verbatim; 'expand its scale as it goes' is the page's own wording.

verdicts.trueWording: I thrilled at how she turned thought problems into intricate cultures, working from the big picture down to the minutiae of local life
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched. Quote verbatim, and the surrounding clause makes it worldbuilding method, matching the claim's framing.

verdicts.trueWording: filling books with pleasurable details like the "common table implement" on Gethen "with which you crack the ice that has formed on your drink between drafts"
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched. Quote verbatim; the Gethenian ice-cracking table implement is cited immediately after, exactly as the claim says.

verdicts.trueWording: I loved Le Guin's worldbuilding, with her well-made ecologies and cultures tied to the unique geographies evoked in her hand-drawn maps
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched. Quote verbatim and the 'hand-drawn maps' limb continues the same clause on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: For the most part, for me, rhythm is something that appears (and surprises me) by way of a lot of editing.
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (Substack, HTTP 200). Quote verbatim in Saunders's answer. The 'rather than by plan' limb is supported by the immediately preceding sentence: writers who 'start out with some idea about a rhythm they want to attain (a plan, or schematic vision)... but that's not true for me.'

verdicts.trueWording: But the rhythm of prose is something that not very many people have studied. The rhythms are so subtle and have to be irregular.
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched. Quote verbatim, and it sits inside the reader's question, which opens 'In an interview with author Ursula Le Guin' and reports her in paraphrase -- both limbs (reader paraphrase; Le Guin interview) supported.

verdicts.trueWording: She does a fantastic job of presenting the story with this mystical air about it. The voice she uses gives it an almost biblical rhythm.
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched. Spoken by Valerie in the transcript; page states 'Your Writers' Room editors are Valerie Francis... and Leslie Watts', so the 'Story Grid editor' limb is supported. Quote verbatim, about A Wizard of Earthsea.

verdicts.trueWording: I think this editorial omniscient POV is the hardest to pull off... This POV choice creates a huge emotional gap between the reader and protagonist.
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched. Quote verbatim in Valerie's section; she names the POV 'editorial omniscient' two sentences earlier, so the claim's POV limb is supported.

verdicts.trueWording: 3. What is the point of view / narrative device? Point of View: Editorial Omniscient
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched. Article bylined 'By Leslie Watts'; the label appears verbatim in the Editor's Six Core Questions analysis, question 3, for A Wizard of Earthsea.

verdicts.trueWording: Tolkien's references to places, people, events (often of long ago) that are not part of the immediate story: these give the reader a conviction of the reality of the immediate scene
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched from ursulakleguin.com. Open letter 'Plausibility in Fantasy' to Alexei Mutovkin, signed 'Ursula Le Guin 2005'. Quote verbatim; every limb (Tolkien; places/people/events; not part of the immediate story; conviction of reality) is in the one sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: because it is shown to be part of a much greater landscape, a long history, a whole world of which it is only a glimpse
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched, same letter and same sentence as 223. Quote verbatim. The claim compresses the page's three-item list by dropping 'a whole world', but attaches 'of which it is only a glimpse' exactly as the page does; no limb is unsupported.
